title: Development: a lead you can spend (part 3 of 3)
outcomes: Counts developed pieces on both sides before attacking
Explains why a sacrifice works against an undeveloped army and fails against a developed one
Decides when castling is urgent and when it can wait
Names the conditions that cancel a lead: a developed defender, a safe king square, lost time
Defends against a lead by developing a defender and trading the attacker instead of grabbing pawns

steps.text: Part 3 of 3: Development: a lead you can spend. This part covers A real game; Say it back. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.prompt: White has a queen out and Black has no piece out. Before the next board: which move would you play to add a piece and make a threat at once?

fields.label: My move and the threat it makes:

steps.text: **A real game.** Paris, 1858: Paul Morphy with White against two amateurs who consulted (the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard), played during an opera [R: recalled, not checked against a source here]. The moves are facts, replayed for legality; the full game has its own lesson in the famous games course. Watch one thing: who has pieces out when White starts to sacrifice?

steps.prompt: Predict before the next board: White has queen, bishop, knight and a pinning bishop out and Black's king is in the middle. What sacrifice would you look at, and which Black pieces would you hope are still at home?

fields.label: The sacrifice I would look at:

steps.caption: Black to move. Watch what Black does with his first developed piece in the next few moves.

line.say: Black defends e5 the quiet way and opens his c8 bishop.
White challenges the centre with a pawn.
Black pins the knight on f3 against the queen.
White takes a pawn and leaves the pinned knight attacked.
Black takes the knight, trading his developed bishop for it.
The queen recaptures and looks up the f-file toward f7.
Black takes back. Material is level; White has a queen out, Black has no piece out.

claims.statement: A Black pawn stands on e5 again.
Black's queen's knight is still on b8.

steps.caption: White to move. Black develops one piece and then uses the queen for defence.

line.say: A second White piece comes out, aimed at f7, which only the king guards.
Black develops and blocks the f-file. He attacks the pawn on e4.
The queen attacks b7, while the bishop still aims at f7.
The queen defends both b7 and f7 along the seventh rank, but she blocks the f8 bishop.

claims.statement: After Bc4 the bishop and the queen both attack f7.
The queen on b3 attacks b7.
Black's king's bishop is still on f8.

steps.caption: White to move. Count now: queen and bishop out against queen and knight. The line adds a knight and a bishop and a pin; after it, count again. [I] The engine likes taking the b7 pawn even more than the game move (depth 16, +2.9 against +2.4): a pawn grab can be fine when the lead is large, which is the exception to the Nimzowitsch warning.

line.say: Another White piece joins in. The pawn on e4 is now defended.
Black guards b5 and d5, but his knight on b8 and bishop on f8 are still at home.
The bishop pins the knight on f6 against the queen. Four White pieces are out against two.
Black attacks the bishop with a pawn. It adds no piece.

claims.statement: Black's queen's knight is still on b8.
Black's king's bishop is still on f8.
A Black pawn stands on b5.
At depth 16 the best move is Qxb7 or Nc3, within 60 centipawns.

steps.caption: White to move. The sacrifice: Black's king is in the middle and White's pieces point at it.

line.say: A knight for a pawn. White spends the lead now, before Black can bring his last pieces out.
Black takes the knight.
The bishop takes a second pawn with check along the diagonal to e8.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's best move is Nxb5.
Taking the knight on f6 is at least 1.5 pawns worse.

steps.caption: Black to move, in check. The legal replies are Nbd7, Nfd7, Nc6, Qd7 and Kd8. Each leaves Black far behind (depth 16: all lose at least six pawns). [R] In the game Black chose the one that develops a piece.

line.say: Black blocks with a knight that was still at home. It is now pinned to the king.
White castles long: the king is safe and the rook lands on the d-file against the pinned knight.
Black brings a rook to the d-file to defend the pinned knight.

claims.statement: Black is in check from the bishop on b5.
A Black rook stands on d8.
A White rook stands on d1.
White's king stands on c1.
Every legal reply except Nc6 is within 1.5 pawns of the best, all bad.
At depth 16 White is at least six pawns ahead, whatever Black replies.

steps.prompt: Black's knight on d7 is pinned and White's rook stands on d1. Before the next board: what would you do with the rook, and why does the pin matter?

steps.caption: White to move. The pin on the d7 square decides the next moves.

line.say: The rook takes the pinned knight.
Black recaptures with the rook.
The second rook joins on the same file: White's last piece enters the attack.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's best move is Rxd7.
A White rook stands on d1.

steps.caption: Black to move. The rook on d7 is pinned and attacked twice; Black tries to hold it.

line.say: Black adds the queen to the defence of the pinned rook.
The bishop takes the rook with check.
The knight recaptures. It now stands on d7, blocking the d-file.

claims.statement: A Black knight ends on d7.
The bishop and the rook both attack d7.

steps.caption: White to move: mate in two. White had a lead in development, and the last sacrifice pulled the defender away.

line.say: The queen gives herself up with check along the eighth rank.
The knight must take her, and leaves d7, which blocked the d-file.
The rook reaches d8 with check, protected by the bishop on g5 along the diagonal. The king has no square, so it is mate.

claims.statement: Qb8+ leads to forced mate in two.
The bishop on g5 and the rook on d1 both attack d8.

steps.text: **What decided it.** Before the first sacrifice White had four pieces out and Black two, with a knight and a bishop at home. [I] Black's early bishop trade did not change the count, but the recapture put White's queen on f3 with tempo. After that nearly every White move carried a threat, while Black's replies developed little. Early queen moves are fine when each one makes a threat. Go back through the game and list which White moves threatened something.

steps.prompt: Find the move where Black could still have changed the count. Which move would you have played, and what did it develop?

fields.label: The move I would play instead:

steps.caption: Black to move at move three, the first place the count could have gone differently. The engine (depth 16) likes taking on d4, and the knight moves are close; the bishop pin of the game was about 0.6 pawn worse. [I] The pin develops a piece but gives up a pawn-sized edge for little.

line.say: Black takes the pawn and keeps the centre contested.

claims.statement: Taking on d4, Nd7 or Nf6 are the engine's best moves, within 40 centipawns.
The bishop pin is at least half a pawn worse than the best move.

steps.caption: Black to move at move six, the second place. A queen move that keeps f7 guarded is about 1.3 pawns better than the knight development of the game (depth 16). [I] Here developing a piece was worse than guarding the target. The sacrifices only cashed in these small slips; compare both boards with your own answer above.

line.say: The queen guards f7 along the seventh rank. Black's other pieces can come out next.

claims.statement: Qf6 and Qd7 are the engine's best moves, within 40 centipawns.
The knight development is at least a pawn worse than the best move.

steps.text: **What to remember.** Count pieces that do something, plus castling, on both sides. A lead is the difference. A sacrifice needs a lead, a target few pieces defend, and a king with no safe run. A developed defender or a safe king square cancels it. Waiting shrinks a lead. Build one with threats; defend one by trading the attacker.

**Self-check before you teach it.** Did you say when a lead works and when it fails? Did you give one example a beginner could set on a board? Did you name one mistake, such as grabbing a pawn or leaving a bishop to be fed a trap? Did you say what you counted and how? Say it in your own words; the app does not grade it.
